summary: Discusses the interfaces group of MIB-II and the experience gained from many media-specific MIB modules. It clarifies and extends how network interfaces are described for management. It is on the standards track at the draft standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: Every network plug on a device gets a line in a report card. This sets out what goes on that card so tools can read it the same way.

questions: what is the interfaces group mib
subtitle: How network management describes every network interface, including each layer stacked inside one.

tldr.problem: The original MIB-II interfaces group assumed one simple row per network interface. Real devices stack several layers (such as PPP over HDLC over a serial connector), add and remove interfaces on the fly, and run fast enough to wrap 32-bit counters in minutes.
tldr.mechanism: The Interfaces Group MIB gives each sub-layer its own row in the ifTable and records how the rows stack in the ifStackTable. It also adds 64-bit counters, a high-speed gauge, interface names, new operational states and rules for link traps.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2863 obsoletes RFC 2233 and is a Draft Standard. It has since been updated by RFC 8892.

today: RFC 2863 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2233, and it has been updated by RFC 8892.

sections.title: What the Interfaces Group MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 2863 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) used by Internet network management protocols. Its subject is the managed objects that describe network interfaces. It revisits the interfaces group of MIB-II (RFC 1213) in light of the many media-specific MIB modules written since, and it also folds in the extensions from RFC 1229.

The idea behind the group is that an internetwork protocol such as IP treats everything beneath it as one generic "network interface". The group offers a common set of objects so any interface can be managed the same way, while media-specific MIBs (Ethernet, for example) add objects of their own. Experience showed that the MIB-II model was too simplistic and too static for some of these media, so this memo standardizes how the model evolved.

The module is written in SMIv2. This memo obsoletes RFC 2233, the previous version of the Interfaces Group MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a clipboard where every network plug has a form with the same boxes to fill in. Because every form looks alike, one tool can read them all.

sections.title: Interface Sub-Layers and the Stack
sections.content:
Older MIBs put one row in the ifTable per whole interface. That breaks down when an interface is really several layers. The RFC's example is PPP running over an HDLC link that uses an RS232-like connector, where each layer has its own media-specific MIB.

The RFC also needs to describe multiplexing. Upward multiplexing is shown by MLP, which spreads load over several serial lines but looks like one point-to-point link to the layers above. Downward multiplexing is shown by several PPP instances, each framed in its own X.25 virtual circuit, all running over one fractional T1 channel.

The adopted solution is one conceptual row in the ifTable per sub-layer, plus a new table, the ifStackTable, that uses INTEGER pointers to record which rows are superior and subordinate to which. Two alternatives that kept one row per whole interface were rejected, partly because they could not describe downward multiplexing and would need an ifType value for every combination of layers.

Packet counters are defined as counting what is delivered to, or requested by, a "higher layer". That can be a forwarding module (such as the one in a MAC-layer bridge), a higher sub-layer, or the local IP module at the top of the stack.

For virtual circuits, the memo strongly recommends that connection-oriented sub-layers do not get a row in the ifTable for each circuit, though it allows it where justified.
sections.plainLanguage: A cake with layers is still one cake, but each layer has its own ingredients list. The stack table is the note that says which layer sits on which.

sections.title: The Four Tables
sections.content:
The MIB consists of four tables.

  • ifTable: the ifTable from MIB-II.
  • ifXTable: objects added by the Interface Evolution effort, replacements for original ifTable objects whose semantics changed significantly, and objects that were previously in the ifExtnsTable.
  • ifStackTable: the relationships among the sub-layers of an interface.
  • ifRcvAddressTable: the media-level addresses the interface will receive. It is generic, so designers of media-specific MIBs must define exactly how it applies to theirs.

Not every object makes sense for every kind of interface. About half the objects in the ifTable apply to all interfaces, including bit-oriented and character-oriented ones. The RFC avoids splitting the ifTable, which would force changes in nearly every SNMP agent. Instead it uses SMIv2 compliance statements over separate object groups: ifGeneralInformationGroup for all interfaces, ifPacketGroup for packet-oriented ones and ifFixedLengthGroup for character-oriented and fixed-length interfaces such as ATM.

Because the object definitions keep the same semantics and wire encodings, they keep the OBJECT IDENTIFIER values assigned by MIB-II, so existing agents generally need no rewrite.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four notebooks: one with the basic facts, one with extra facts, one showing which layers sit on which, and one listing the addresses the plug listens for.

sections.title: Interface Numbering and Names
sections.content:
Each interface is identified by ifIndex, which must stay constant at least until the management system is next re-initialized. MIB-II also limited ifIndex to no more than ifNumber, which is a problem when interfaces are added and removed dynamically. This memo deletes that limit and keeps ifNumber unchanged. The result can be "holes" in the ifTable, which SNMP GetNext and GetBulk handle easily. The RFC admits this change breaks a few management applications but judges that preferable to breaking all agents. It recommends keeping ifIndex values small, starting at 1.

A dynamically removed interface's ifIndex must not be reused by a different interface until after the next re-initialization of the network management system.

When an interface returns but its counters were interrupted, the new object ifCounterDiscontinuityTime records the last discontinuity. A manager must discard any counter difference computed across two polls where that value differs, in addition to checking sysUpTime.

With a row per sub-layer, mapping rows to physical ports gets harder. So ifName holds the device's local name for the interface (for example "wan1"), and ifAlias is a non-volatile name a manager can assign, which must survive reboots. The existing ifDescr remains a description.
sections.plainLanguage: Each plug has a number on its sticker. Plugs can come and go, so the number is never given to a different plug in the meantime, and you can also write a nickname on it that sticks.

sections.title: Counter Size and Interface Speed
sections.content:
As links get faster, a 32-bit counter wraps sooner. The RFC says a 10Mbs stream of back-to-back, full-size packets wraps ifInOctets in just over 57 minutes. At 100Mbs the minimum wrap time is 5.7 minutes, and at 1Gbs it is 34 seconds. Scaling the counters was rejected because slow traffic would then look bursty. Instead the memo adds 64-bit "high capacity" counters in new groups (ifHCFixedLengthGroup, ifHCPacketGroup and ifVHCPacketGroup).

The old 32-bit counters are not deprecated and MUST still be available when 64-bit ones are in use, reporting the low 32 bits of the 64-bit count. The requirements depend on speed, as the table shows.

Speed has the same problem. ifSpeed tops out at (2**31)-1 bits per second, about 2.2Gbs. The new ifHighSpeed reports speed in units of 1,000,000 bits per second, so the true speed is the reported value plus or minus 500,000 bits per second.

Separate multicast and broadcast counters now replace the combined non-unicast counters, which are deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: An odometer that only has a few digits flips back to zero quickly if you drive fast. The fix is a bigger odometer, but only for the fast cars.

sections.title: Interface Status and Link Traps
sections.content:
Three states are added to ifOperStatus: dormant (waiting for an external event, as for on-demand interfaces), notPresent (down because a component, typically hardware, is missing) and lowerLayerDown (down because an interface below it in the stack is down). The meaning of down now depends on ifAdminStatus. If the admin status is not down and the operational status is down, a fault is presumed. If admin status is down, operational status normally is too, without necessarily a fault.

When an interface in the middle of a stack is considered, its status is up if any interface beneath it lets it pass packets, and lowerLayerDown while every interface below it is down, notPresent, lowerLayerDown or testing.

linkUp and linkDown traps are generated just after ifOperStatus leaves, or just before it enters, the down state. They are never generated on transitions to or from notPresent, and lowerLayerDown counts as equivalent to down for this purpose. An agent should limit the rate of traps when an interface is flapping. Because each sub-layer could trap, the new ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable object lets managers choose; by default only the lowest sub-layer generates traps.

Finally, an agent MUST NOT instantiate an object with an incorrect value. If it cannot count something it must answer with an error such as noSuchInstance, not report zero, so managers must cope with missing columns in a row.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic light can be green, red, or waiting for a car to arrive. Here the report card says which, and the alarm only rings when the light turns to red or comes back from red.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects in this MIB have a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. Writable objects let an administrator control interfaces and run tests on them, so unauthorized access could cause denial of service or, combined with other breaches such as physical ones, unauthorized connectivity to a device.

The RFC points out that SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, even on a secure network such as one protected with IPSec, because there is no control over who may GET or SET objects. It recommends that implementers consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). Configuring the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can read or change instances is left to the customer or user.
sections.plainLanguage: Some boxes on the report card can be changed, not just read. Only the right people should hold the pencil, or someone could switch a plug off.
